title: Bhotekoshi glacier collapse and debris flood, Nepal (August 2026)
story: On the morning of 26 August 2026, rock and glacier ice broke off Langtang Lirung and briefly dammed the river. The flood that followed swept down the Bhote Koshi through Rasuwagadhi, Timure and Syabrubesi, killing more than 1,400 people
method: Coherence measures how similar the ground's radar fingerprint is between two passes 12 days apart. Ground that was ripped up, buried or flooded in between loses coherence, so a drop compared with the usual coherence marks where the flood went
image_corners_order: top-left, top-right, bottom-right, bottom-left, as [lon, lat]

coherence_baseline.legend: usual coherence before the event, 0 (purple, always changing) to 1 (yellow, stable)

coherence_change.legend: red: coherence dropped below normal by 0.15 or more, fully red from 0.3

hv_darkening.legend: blue: HV darker after the event by 1.5 dB or more (vegetation lost)

hh_change.legend: red brighter, blue darker after the event, changes over 1.5 dB

stages.headline: NISAR was watching the valley every few days
stages.summary: Before 26 August, NISAR passed over the valley every few days. Each pass is compared with the one 12 days earlier: where the ground stays the same, the radar picture stays the same too. Through June, July and August the valley looked normal, steady on the slopes and always changing on the snow and ice. The last pass before the collapse was on 19 August

stages.headline: The flood path shows up as ground that changed

metric.label: Ground that changed more than usual

stages.summary: Comparing the passes on 19 August and 31 August, the valley floor changed along a 44 km line, from the collapse site below Langtang Lirung, through Rasuwagadhi and Timure, to Syabrubesi. That is the path of the debris flood: ground torn up, buried or scoured between the two passes

stages.headline: Radar maps the damage through cloud, within days
stages.summary: Radar sees through monsoon cloud, day or night, so within a week of the collapse NISAR had mapped the whole flood path. Along the river, the radar signal from vegetation dropped over about 15 km², where trees and plants were stripped away. 2 days after the collapse, NISAR moved the area to Urgent Response, processing new passes faster
actions: Use 12-day coherence to map damage along a valley soon after a collapse, even under monsoon cloud
Keep regular passes over hanging glaciers above inhabited valleys
